听.title: Who does the housework? (BBC 6 Minute English · Ep.260813)
听.body:
BBC 6 Minute English — Who does the housework? (Episode 260813 / 13 Aug 2026)

Neil: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Neil.
Pippa: And I'm Pippa. When it comes to household chores, jobs like cleaning, washing clothes or looking after the kids, it's often women who do most of the work. Here, two female listeners of BBC World Service programme People Fixing the World share their experiences. Do they sound familiar to you?

Listener 1: I do everything. I do all the house chores, I do the food shopping, I do all the cooking, I clean the bathroom.
Listener 2: Are the chores done equally between me and my husband? No, they're not done equally. I do most of the chores.

Pippa: So, you're a family man, Neil. Do you do your fair share of household chores?
Neil: I think so. My wife works part time and I work full time, so when I'm not working, I do things, and when she's not working, she does things.
Pippa: Yeah, it's similar in my house, so me and my husband try to split things, but it's difficult, isn't it?

Pippa: Figures from UN Women suggest that every day women around the world spend three hours more than men on unpaid care and domestic work. So, in this episode, we'll be hearing about two projects helping husbands and wives share the housework more fairly.

Neil: But now I have a question for you, Pippa. According to a survey by Good Housekeeping magazine earlier this year, what is the most hated household chore in Britain? a) deep cleaning the oven, b) scrubbing the toilet, or c) cleaning the windows?
Pippa: I'm going to say deep cleaning the oven because I really hate that job.

Neil: The first project is on the remote Indonesian island of Rote. Men traditionally work as rice farmers or fishermen, while women look after the home, the children and older people. But with few washing machines and no running water, these domestic chores take a long time.
Pippa: The NGO ARUNGI runs a project trying to change attitudes. Mama Shilpa, a community leader, explains: "It is expected that the tasks done in the house — holding the child, feeding the child, washing dishes, cooking — will all be done by the mother."
Neil: On Rote, cleaning, cooking and sweeping are considered women's work — a negative term for boring and repetitive tasks traditionally done by women.

Pippa: Research suggests women in wealthy countries also spend much more time on unpaid care work. In Croatia, the NGO Status M runs their Superdads project. Project worker Anamarija Sočo leads workshops encouraging dads and sons to take pressure off mums.
Anamarija Sočo: "Mothers have more space for their careers, or hobbies, or just simply to rest — I mean, just to take a breather. Women tend to especially appreciate men who do these kinds of chores. And when they start pulling their weight, then they jokingly say that women tend to nag less."

Pippa: Both NGO projects agree: men doing more around the house results in happier homes. So, what was the answer to your quiz, Neil?
Neil: The most hated chore in Britain is cleaning the windows — 23% of people said so.

Vocabulary:
- chores: household tasks like cleaning, washing and ironing that have to be done regularly.
- fair share: a reasonable amount that you should do.
- women's work: a negative term for boring, repetitive tasks stereotypically done by women.
- division of labour: a way of organising work where different tasks are done by different groups of people.
- take a breather: (idiom) to stop what you're doing for a short time and rest.
- pull your weight: to work as hard as everyone else doing the same job.

Transcript source: BBC Learning English (not a word-for-word transcript). Quiz answer: cleaning the windows.
听.zh: 本期讨论'谁做家务'：BBC 听众分享经验，印尼 Rote 岛与克罗地亚的 NGO 项目推动夫妻更公平分担家务。quiz 答案：英国人最讨厌的家务是擦窗户（23% 受访者）。重点词汇：chores（家务）、fair share（公平分担）、women's work（女性专属的重复性杂活）、division of labour（劳动分工）、take a breather（歇口气）、pull your weight（尽本分）。

说.title: Speaking · Share the load at home
说.body: Describe how chores are divided in your household. Do you think the division is fair? Tell a story about a chore you hate most and how you cope with it. Try to use at least three of today's phrases: 'do my fair share', 'pull your weight', 'take a breather', 'division of labour'.
说.zh: 描述你家里家务如何分配，你觉得公平吗？讲一件你最讨厌的家务以及你是怎么应付的。尽量用上今天至少三个短语：do my fair share / pull your weight / take a breather / division of labour。

读.title: Growth driver shifts from bricks to bits (China Daily · 2026-08-17)
读.body:
Growth driver shifts from bricks to bits
China Daily | 2026-08-17 | By a former prime minister of Mongolia

If you want to understand where the world is heading, stop looking at the skyscraper cranes in Beijing and start looking at the 5G base stations in the countryside. For decades, the story of China was the story of "hard infrastructure" — concrete, steel and a property market that seemed like it would never stop climbing. But something fundamental has changed.

While the world was busy watching China's real estate sector contract by 0.2 percent and its construction industry dip by 4 percent in the first half of 2026, the country was quietly finishing a massive rewiring of its entire economic base. China's GDP still grew by a steady 4.7 percent to reach 69.57 trillion yuan ($10.31 trillion) in the first half of 2026, but the engines driving that growth weren't bulldozers — they were algorithms.

China is building a new kind of "central nervous system" for its society. By July 2026, the country had installed 5.1 million 5G base stations. That's not just a statistic; it's a platform. It has applied 5G and gigabit optical networks across 94 major categories of the national economy. And it isn't stopping there. It has already made significant strides in verifying 6G system architecture.

The second layer of this rewiring is energy. China didn't just meet its 2030 wind and solar power targets — it crushed them six years early in 2024. By the end of July 2026, its solar capacity hit a staggering 1,274 gigawatts. When your nonfossil energy consumption exceeds crude oil for the first time in history — as China did in 2024 — you are no longer just an oil importer; you are an exporter of the future.

On July 17, 2026, President Xi Jinping stood up at the World AI Conference in Shanghai and essentially offered to share the "operating system" of this new era with the rest of the world. He called AI a "symphony of international cooperation" rather than a solo act. That's not just building a coalition; that's building the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, headquartered in Shanghai with 29 founding members.

While some are trying to build an "AI Iron Curtain", China is pitching an open-source model where intelligence is a public good, not a private commodity. The core conclusion is this: China is betting that if you automate the basics, you change the "superstructure" of society itself.
读.zh: 文章指出，中国经济增长引擎正从'钢筋水泥'转向'数智动力'：截至2026年7月已建成510万个5G基站，非化石能源消费首超原油；中国把 AI 称为国际合作的'交响乐'而非独奏，并向全球南方开放开源智能与绿色能源。核心结论：自动化基础，将重塑社会'上层建筑'。

写.title: Writing · From hard infrastructure to a 'central nervous system'
写.body: Write 150–200 words on this prompt: 'Some say a country's strength used to be measured in concrete and steel; today it is measured in algorithms and green energy. Do you agree? Use evidence from the article and your own observation.'
写.zh: 写一篇150–200词：有人认为一国实力过去看钢筋水泥，今天看算法与绿色能源，你同意吗？结合文章证据与你自己的观察展开。

练.title: Practice · Phrases & grammar
练.body: 1) Fill in: 'My roommate never ___ his ___ — I end up doing all the dishes.' (pull / weight)  2) Rewrite using 'division of labour': 'Men farm, women cook and clean.'  3) Make a sentence with 'take a breather'.  4) Grammar: 'By July 2026, China had installed 5.1 million 5G base stations.' → Identify the tense and say why it is used.
练.zh: 1) 填空：pull his weight。2) 改写：There is a clear division of labour — men work in the fields while women cook and clean. 3) 造句：After two hours of studying, I took a breather with a cup of tea. 4) 语法：过去完成时（past perfect），表示在2026年7月这一过去时间点之前已经完成的动作。
